entry.content:
Creative Insight

How brands are showing up in the real world

The next generation of brand experiences isn’t necessarily about building bigger worlds, it’s about getting better at showing up in real life

By Rebecca Fulleylove 25/11/2026 6:28 am

The brand pop-up has been one of marketing’s most reliable physical formats. But as audiences have become more familiar with its mechanics, the experience has started to feel less distinctive.

The brands looking to make physical experiences count are becoming more thoughtful about what they are actually for. Rather than creating an entirely branded world and asking people to step inside it, they are borrowing from the places, rituals and communities that already exist – markets, bodegas, run clubs, neighbourhood shops – and finding ways to become a part of them.

For skincare brand The Ordinary, early this summer, that meant bringing its global Markup Marché concept to Old Spitalfields Market in London. Working with experience agency Heaps + Stacks alongside Uncommon Creative Studio, the skincare brand transplanted its stripped-back, black-and-white identity into the colourful chaos of a British fruit and vegetable stall.

entry.title: Fireside builds ‘worst hiking trail on earth’ for eco-campaign
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Fireside builds ‘worst hiking trail on earth’ for eco-campaign The Great Victorian Fckery Trail highlights the environmental destruction happening in Victoria, Australia with an unorthodox walk ahead of the state election By Charlotte Rawlings 25/11/2026 3:45
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Fireside builds ‘worst hiking trail on earth’ for eco-campaign

The Great Victorian Fckery Trail highlights the environmental destruction happening in Victoria, Australia with an unorthodox walk ahead of the state election

By Charlotte Rawlings 25/11/2026 3:45 am

Melbourne’s Fireside Agency has created “the worst hiking trail on earth” for environmental coalition Victorians for Nature to spotlight how wildlife is in crisis ahead of Victoria’s state election.

The Great Victorian Fckery Trail is available on AllTrails, an app where people can plan their walks, and is part of Victorians for Nature’s Stop the F*ckery campaign.

Fireside developed Stop the F*ckery with Victorians for Nature earlier this year to track “forest, feral, fish, fauna and funding f*ckery” ahead of the state election.

In a bid to target nature lovers who aren’t following the fight, The Great Victorian Fckery Trail is a 45km route leading walkers to 21 sites where the devastation is impacting Victoria’s forests, grasslands, oceans and parks.

It includes stops like the stump of a felled three metre-wide Mountain Grey Gum, bulldozed protected grasslands, a dingo kill zone and a state park slated for a luge-style rollercoaster.

Walkers can tackle any of the trail’s five sections on foot or explore all 21 stops in the app, with each waypoint detailing the damage done to the site. The Stop the F*ckery website then encourages users to tell their local candidates what they saw before the election on November 28.

Lauren Haberfield, director of creativity at Fireside Agency, said: “We were mapping all these sites where Victoria’s nature was being wrecked. So we thought, why not send people to see them? Everyone cares about nature in the abstract. It gets a lot harder to ignore when you’re standing in the middle of the destruction.”

The work is part of Fireside’s new story activation offering, which turns a narrative into something people can experience, such as an event, an object or a place. The offering is led by Haberfield, who joined Fireside from Edelman France, where she was executive creative director.

Ben Hart, managing director at Fireside, added: “Most of what we make for clients gets read. We want more of it to be experienced. The worst hiking trail on earth seemed like a good place to start.”

entry.title: Visa global brand refresh by Base Design spotlights progress
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Visa global brand refresh by Base Design spotlights progress The revamped visual identity will run across multiple communications, featuring a fresh symbol, a graphic device and a bespoke typeface By Charlotte Rawlings 25/11/2026 1:23 am Visa has unveiled a r
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Visa global brand refresh by Base Design spotlights progress

The revamped visual identity will run across multiple communications, featuring a fresh symbol, a graphic device and a bespoke typeface

By Charlotte Rawlings 25/11/2026 1:23 am

Visa has unveiled a refreshed global identity by creative studio Base Design that centres on the idea of progress.

It is the card payment brand’s first significant refresh since 2021, and Base Design set out to make it relevant for the next generation without losing what makes Visa so recognisable.

The redesign is rooted in the notion that progress looks different for everyone, and that Visa is there to support its customers at every scale, from a contactless coffee on the way to work to a trip abroad.

Base Design created a new brand symbol, a signature graphic device and a bespoke typeface as part of a flexible visual identity.

Built for digital and motion, the symbol takes the simple form of the letter V, drawn directly from the company’s wordmark and retaining Visa’s signature wingtip. The letter V will begin to appear on select credit cards and across Visa’s digital properties to offer a more compact expression of the brand.

A hero graphic device injects the system with a sense of forward momentum. It can feature the wordmark, the V, or messaging, and is partially cropped at the bar’s right-hand edge in a subtle nod to Visa’s established branding. The graphic creates the impression that Visa is always pulling progress forward while giving the brand a premium aesthetic.

Visa Sans, a typeface created with Displaay Type Foundry, ties the whole system together. Inspired by the Visa wordmark, the typography extends the logo’s character across the wider identity.

As part of the redesign, Base Design built three levels of visual expression: a core identity for everyday needs, an extended version for deeper storytelling and custom “stretched” treatments designed for high-impact experiences.

Social campaigns have the freedom to embrace colour and motion, while communications for banking partners can stay restrained, and premium experiences can take a more subtle approach.

Min Lew, managing partner and ECD at Base Design, said: “Our ambition was to build on Visa’s extraordinary equity while giving it a renewed sense of energy and expression, one that feels as relevant to the next generation as it does to the generations who have grown up with it.”

The system is being rolled out across motion, sonic branding and iconography, alongside dedicated sub-identities such as Visa Infinite.

The new design has been built for everyday touchpoints because Visa often appears in people’s lives for only a fleeting moment, such as on a card or at checkout. It will be seen on tap-to-pay animations and security iconography to ‘Visa accepted here’ decals and merchant materials.

Lew added: “The most powerful identities are built on simple ideas with extraordinary depth. With Visa, we translated their role of championing everyday progress into a distinctive graphic expression.

“More than a framing device, the hero graphic device brings movement, direction, and possibility to the identity. This simple gesture becomes the foundation for a visual language that can be energetic at a global sporting event, confident and bold in a B2B environment, or vibrant and elevated for affluent audiences. Each expression is distinct, yet unmistakably Visa.”

entry.content:
Creative Insight

The Monthly Interview: Cat How

As How+How expands its presence in the US, takes on larger clients and explores the possibilities of AI, its co-founder explains why she’s determined to keep turning up the volume

By Adam Woodward 24/11/2026 3:41 am

“Sometimes you go into a project thinking it’s going to be one thing, and the people involved open up a completely different possibility,” says Cat How of How+How, the independent branding and design agency she co-founded with her partner Rog in 2020.

An open-minded approach, How believes, sets up a project for success. But the trick to unearthing the idea that makes a business, product or place distinctive? “Tell your truth,” as the studio’s favourite saying goes. Then, keep “dialling it up until it’s impossible to ignore.”

“We settled on the idea of truth because I think it’s a really sticky word at the moment,” she explains of the core value at the heart of How+How’s strategy. “Ultimately, it’s about finding the truth in the client’s story and amplifying it.”

entry.title: KFC campaign puts a saucy twist on Indian cinematic storytelling
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration KFC campaign puts a saucy twist on Indian cinematic storytelling Directed by Bruno Bossi, Drip Happens centres around a traditional Indian matchmaking meeting known as a rishta – with unexpectedly comic results By Daniel Milroy Maher 24/11/2026 3:04 am To cel
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

KFC campaign puts a saucy twist on Indian cinematic storytelling

Directed by Bruno Bossi, Drip Happens centres around a traditional Indian matchmaking meeting known as a rishta – with unexpectedly comic results

By Daniel Milroy Maher 24/11/2026 3:04 am

To celebrate the recent launch of its Korean Dunked Range, KFC India has released a new campaign film titled Drip Happens, which sees the cultural and culinary worlds of Korea and India collide in a saucy showdown.

Developed by agency Mad About Digital and directed by Bruno Bossi, who won gold at Cannes Lions in 2025 for his KFC Thailand spot Let There Be Cake, this latest effort revolves around a rishta (a traditional Indian matchmaking meeting), where two families have come together in the hope of uniting a young couple.

The only problem is that the groom-to-be is Korean, and the prospective bride’s aunt doesn’t approve of the match. Determined to mess it up, she offers the man a piece of Korean Dunked chicken, before sneakily nudging him so that he sends it flying through the air.

As it hurtles across the room, it sprays the people and furniture in the room with special gochujang sauce, before landing perfectly in the bride’s outstretched hand – sealing the deal, rather than breaking it.

At once silly and dramatic, Drip Happens adopts the over-the-top tone that has become synonymous with Indian cinema. Commenting on this approach, Bossi said: “I’ve always admired Indian film culture from a distance, so the chance to step inside it and play with its genres and characters was a real treat.

“Working in a new cultural space frees you from the usual rules, and with a line like ‘Drip Happens’, we had the perfect excuse to turn the drama all the way up.”

The new campaign film forms part of a larger brand platform, which will carry future Dunked launches, and continue to celebrate the idea that great taste is worth spilling some sauce over.

entry.title: Byron rebrand by Interstate celebrates British character
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Byron rebrand by Interstate celebrates British character The agency explored the burger chain’s history and place in the UK market before landing on Gothic typography, whimsical illustrations and a cool colour palette By Charlotte Rawlings 24/11/2026 3:03 am
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Byron rebrand by Interstate celebrates British character

The agency explored the burger chain’s history and place in the UK market before landing on Gothic typography, whimsical illustrations and a cool colour palette

By Charlotte Rawlings 24/11/2026 3:03 am

Interstate Creative Partners has leaned into modern British character in a bid to reposition and reinvent British hamburger restaurant chain Byron.

The rebrand aims to attract a new generation of customers to Byron, which now has backing from private equity firm Niyamo Capital, and arrives following a turbulent decade for the chain, with numerous controversies and site closures.

A fresh logo is inspired by historic Blackletter typography while a clean colour palette combines black, white and blue. This system will work consistently across restaurants, packaging, uniforms, digital platforms and social media.

Illustration and a conversational tone of voice aim to bring warmth and eccentricity to the chain, while documentary-style photography prioritises real people and real food rather than the more polished assets often seen in the category.

Alex Chadwick, client services and strategy director at Interstate, said: “We wanted Byron to be confident without showing off and witty without trying too hard, with those principles shaping every customer touchpoint. This sense of the British spirit was an inspiration for the brand’s direction.”

Interstate began the process by diving into Byron’s history, interviewing leadership, surveying employees and benchmarking more than 30 competitors. The brand consultancy also teamed up with cultural forecasting agency The Future Laboratory to monitor changing British perspectives on value, provenance and national identity.

According to Interstate, the findings revealed that Byron had strong brand recognition but diminishing meaning. This was due to multiple ownership changes and rebrands leaving Byron with seven restaurants operating under separate visual identities.

Moreover, Interstate found Byron had built itself on start-up energy and prided itself on personality. In addition, the mid-range burger market often defaults to an Americanised experience, which led to Interstate advising the restaurant to celebrate its British heritage.

Chadwick added: “Successful rebrands don’t begin with logos, they begin with understanding why a business matters. Our role is to uncover what makes a brand distinctive, then express that consistently through strategy, creativity and technical execution. Only when every element works together can a brand perform better.”

entry.summary: Creative Inspiration DNCO designs wayfinding system for the Natural History Museum The refreshed system, which features adaptable signage and a new map, aims to make navigation clearer for visitors By Charlotte Rawlings 23/11/2026 3:55 am London-based Branding agency DNCO has cre
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

DNCO designs wayfinding system for the Natural History Museum

The refreshed system, which features adaptable signage and a new map, aims to make navigation clearer for visitors

By Charlotte Rawlings 23/11/2026 3:55 am

London-based Branding agency DNCO has created 400 signs and a redesigned map for the Natural History Museum to help visitors navigate the attraction.

The revamped wayfinding system is now installed in the museum’s Grade I-listed central London home and its sister site at Tring in Hertfordshire.

The challenge was to simplify the journey throughout the museum without diminishing the character of Alfred Waterhouse’s original design of the South Kensington location, which dates back to 1881.

Instead of adding more information, DNCO’s strategy establishes what visitors need to know, and when. The museum’s five-zone framework, developed by Endpoint, divides the estate into manageable areas. DNCO gave each zone its own colour, which appears consistently across every map and sign from the entrance maps to the gallery door.

Upon arrival, welcome signs introduce the zones and the wider collection, while directional signs further guide visitors through the zones. Meanwhile, guests are greeted at each gallery by special identification signs, which are new to the museum. Bespoke illustrations depicting what the galleries have to offer were designed by the Natural History Museum’s in-house team.

Research found that the existing map, which used a one-point perspective view, distorted the relationship between spaces and levels.

DNCO tested isometric views, but found that the more accurately the map described the building, the harder it became to read. Instead, they opted to strip back the architectural detail to create a simplified plan featuring only what visitors need to orient themselves. This pared-back approach extends outdoors to include the replanted gardens in the fifth zone.

The project was announced in 2023, when the museum invited agencies to tender for a new signage and wayfinding system across its two sites. According to the museum, DNCO’s work is the first major overhaul since 2007. In the years between, new signs had been added alongside the old with no real consistency.

Every element of the system had to work within the constraints of listed architecture. DNCO worked with heritage officers at the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea to protect the building during the process, overseeing pull-tests of existing fixing holes and designing flexible backplates that reuse them wherever possible.

DNCO also ensured the signage could adapt to events and exhibitions at the museum. Directional signs carry an updatable panel that promotes temporary exhibitions, while welcome signs and donation points are freestanding and on wheels, so galleries can be cleared for evening events.

Sign faces are removable, recyclable aluminium honeycomb panels that in-house teams can update as galleries and exhibitions change.

Patrick Eley, executive creative director at DNCO, said: “Designing signage for the Natural History Museum is a bit like trying to organise an ant colony. Only the ants are seven years old, wearing hi-viz jackets and all looking for the dinosaurs.

“With seven million annual visitors and 140 years of buildings to navigate, it’s a long day out. But a museum isn’t an airport. We wanted to help people find what they came for, while at the same time making sure they didn’t miss everything else worth discovering along the way.”

entry.title: KitKat Vietnam sneaks break reminders into developers’ code
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration KitKat Vietnam sneaks break reminders into developers’ code Leo Vietnam has created an AI prompt that transforms the equals sign, which looks a lot like a KitKat, into a visual prompt for workers to recharge By Charlotte Rawlings 23/11/2026 3:34 am KitKat Vie
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

KitKat Vietnam sneaks break reminders into developers’ code

Leo Vietnam has created an AI prompt that transforms the equals sign, which looks a lot like a KitKat, into a visual prompt for workers to recharge

By Charlotte Rawlings 23/11/2026 3:34 am

KitKat Vietnam has met workers where they are to encourage them to step away from their screens during the working day with a handy piece of code.

Created in collaboration with Leo Vietnam, Kit=Code leans into the brand’s message ‘Have a break, have a KitKat’ and transforms the equals sign in coding into a contextual cue to take a breather.

The work is inspired by the fact developers type the symbol countless times a day. When KitKat noticed the two parallel lines resembled two of its chocolate biscuit fingers, the brand saw an opportunity to bring its slogan into people’s working environment.

Every equals sign appearing in a line of code becomes a signal that accumulates over time. Once a certain threshold is reached, a break reminder appears.

Kit=Code is an AI prompt designed to work alongside coding assistants. Developers can access the feature by simply visiting the microsite nghixahoi.vn, where they can copy the Kit=Code prompt and paste it into Claude or Codex, AI coding assistants commonly used by developers.

The tool tracks the time spent coding and how often the equals sign appears in their code, displaying break reminders when progress reaches 30%, 50% and 100%, allowing coders to pause and recharge.

When the 100% milestone is reached and the break reminder appears, developers will receive a GrabMart Vietnam voucher, which can be redeemed on KitKat products at convenience stores across the country.

Kit=Code was introduced to the public through content across YouTube, Facebook and TikTok. Teasers take inspiration from the coding world with a red background, pixelated images and various symbols.

Thiti ‘Moss’ Boonkerd, executive creative director at Leo Vietnam, said: “There are more developers among our friends and acquaintances than we might think. They are behind many of the conveniences we use every day, making all our lives easier.

“Yet they often forget to take a moment for themselves. With Kit=Code, we wanted to place that reminder right where they spend most of their time – within their lines of code – using a symbol that looks just like two KitKat fingers. Sometimes, the simplest reminder to take a break is right in front of us.”

entry.summary: Creative Insight Should creatives care more about advertising history? As a junior creative, it was essential for Ben Kay to know the great ads of the past. But, he reflects, does this really matter now, when advertising today looks so different? By Ben Kay 23/11/2026 3:03 am Wha
entry.content:
Creative Insight

Should creatives care more about advertising history?

As a junior creative, it was essential for Ben Kay to know the great ads of the past. But, he reflects, does this really matter now, when advertising today looks so different?

By Ben Kay 23/11/2026 3:03 am

What would you think if you met a film director who hadn’t heard of Citizen Kane? Or a classical pianist who was unaware of Beethoven’s Fifth? How about a sculptor who had never seen Michelangelo’s David? You’d probably wonder how someone could pursue a career in a creative discipline without knowing the great work that helped define it.

I’m not saying we should spend years slavishly worshipping the classics, but surely a basic understanding of the best of what came before is a fundamental part of learning how to do something to a high standard.

And yet, in advertising, it’s not unusual to encounter people who seem to have very little knowledge of the industry’s past excellence, including some who are enthusiastically filling LinkedIn with ideas that first saw the light of day 20 or 30 years ago.

I occasionally point out the similarities, and although creatives from my generation seem to appreciate my efforts, I’ve discovered that informing someone that their brilliant new concept isn’t that new after all doesn’t tend to go down terribly well. But are younger creatives becoming less familiar with the great ads of the past, and if so, does it matter?

entry.title: Why brands are hungry for Min KyungJin
entry.summary: Creative Process Why brands are hungry for Min KyungJin The South Korean artist, also known as Sibatable, has built a practice around transforming food into unexpected objects. She talks to CR about bringing her distinctive approach to commercial work By Rebecca Fulleylove 20/11/
entry.content:
Creative Process

Why brands are hungry for Min KyungJin

The South Korean artist, also known as Sibatable, has built a practice around transforming food into unexpected objects. She talks to CR about bringing her distinctive approach to commercial work

By Rebecca Fulleylove 20/11/2026 7:20 am

“Food is hard to control. But if I control it too much, it starts to feel like a craft. Whatever I’m trying to express, I need it to still feel like food,” says culinary artist Min Kyungjin. “So I try to find a way through cooking, but sometimes I hit a dead end. When that happens, I write it down and pass it on to my future self.” Sometimes, with a little more experience, she figures it out.

Working under the moniker Sibatable, Kyungjin’s food creations have lit up the internet since she began sharing them in 2022. Having studied culinary arts at university, the South Korea-based creative was looking for an outlet. “Rather than showing myself, I expressed the things I loved through food and posted them on Instagram,” she says.  “The materials were all right there in my fridge.  Sharing those creations and connecting with people gradually grew into the work I do today.”

At first, she simply made things she liked – dogs, cats, rice koalas lying under an egg blanket. But the practice has since become even more playful, moving towards inanimate objects and everyday items like handbags, perfume bottles and socks, though the cute animals still make a welcome appearance.

entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Andstudio creates maritime-inspired identity for Rotterdam bistro Werf’s rebrand aims to marry the location’s industrial past with contemporary urban life By Charlotte Rawlings 20/11/2026 3:03 am Vilnius-based creative agency andstudio has created a visual id
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Andstudio creates maritime-inspired identity for Rotterdam bistro

Werf’s rebrand aims to marry the location’s industrial past with contemporary urban life

By Charlotte Rawlings 20/11/2026 3:03 am

Vilnius-based creative agency andstudio has created a visual identity for Werf, a bar and bistro in Rotterdam, inspired by the destination’s industrial heritage and maritime setting.

Following its launch in autumn 2025, Werf’s revamped branding is part of a bid to bring the docklands closer to contemporary Rotterdam.

Based in Stadsdriehoek, the bistro is located beside a steep working slipway of the Koningspoort in the Oude Haven, where ships are still lowered into the harbour.

The 20-degree slope has informed the visual identity, with the logo, written in bold typography, also following this sharp angle. The inspiration does not stop at the ramps and slipways of Rotterdam, as the slanted text also pays homage to the raising of a glass or the tilt of a champagne bottle during fermentation.

Augustinas Paukštė, co-founder and creative director at andstudio, who led the redesign, said they didn’t want to “overcomplicate” the identity, describing Werf as “an honest, simple place”.

“We built the whole identity on one thing: the 20-degree angle of the Koningspoort slipway, where historic ships come out of the water to be restored.”

Seasonal colour palettes also pay homage to the ships docked at the wharf. The colour scheme of the menu is dictated by whichever ship is docked at the shipyard at the time.

The location gave the bistro its tagline, ‘Alles op de helling’, which translates literally to ‘everything on the slipway’, and figuratively ‘nothing is fixed’.

According to Paukštė, most of the inspiration came from the location itself, such as “the sharp steel structure of the cranes, the dock, and the mechanics of how a ship is pulled onto the slipway and launched back into the water”.

The andstudio team also read books on maritime history and shipbuilding to bring a piece of the working harbour into the bistro. “The hardest part was trusting that one single idea could carry the whole identity. It takes courage not to add more,” said Paukštė.

He also noted that his favourite part of the identity is the door stop, which can be found throughout the restaurant and the kitchen, leveraging the same 20-degree angle with the logo filling the space. “It also doubles as a wedge to level uneven table legs. It is a small detail, but it shows how far simplicity can go.”

He added that Werf’s personality comes through in “roughness and simplicity”. “That is not only the character of the bistro but of maritime culture as a whole: a bit rough around the edges, simple, made for everyone, and very romantic.”

entry.title: Wedge studio on how everything can be special
entry.summary: Creative Leadership Wedge studio on how everything can be special As Montreal and LA-based design studio Wedge reaches its 10th anniversary, it’s more determined, more optimistic, and more punk rock than ever By Emma Tucker 19/11/2026 3:29 am The first thing you see when you land
entry.content:
Creative Leadership

Wedge studio on how everything can be special

As Montreal and LA-based design studio Wedge reaches its 10th anniversary, it’s more determined, more optimistic, and more punk rock than ever

By Emma Tucker 19/11/2026 3:29 am

The first thing you see when you land on Wedge’s website is a simple sentence, emblazoned across the top: Everything Can Be Special. It’s a hopeful statement that feels absolutely right for the work the Montreal and LA design studio makes: clever, craft-steeped, soulful design that tunes into just the right level of nostalgia.

Wedge knows exactly what compels someone to pick up a brand. And they make it look effortless. “We really love what we do,” says co-founder and creative director Sarah Di Domenico. “We’re people who are excited by life, and I think that’s felt in the work. Joy is very important to us; I think it’s a very punk rock decision to choose joy.”

Di Domenico has been involved with the studio almost from the beginning, joining a year after design director Justin Lortie started it in 2016. “They were doing the most incredible work,” she says. “And I was looking through their decks and was like, well, you’re missing the story. That was my part.”

Di Domenico’s background is in the ad industry, creating campaigns for brands including Visa, HBO, Topshop and The North Face – doing the kind of truth-searching, storytelling work that she says would probably now fall under the title of ‘creative strategist’.
